title: Transformers
question: Does the relationship between fast weight programmers and attention support Schmidhuber's claim to priority for the principle of the 2017 Transformer?

usual_credit.summary: Ashish Vaswani and seven co-authors, most of them at Google, introduced the Transformer in 'Attention Is All You Need' at NIPS 2017, a sequence model built from stacked multi-head softmax self-attention layers with positional encodings and no recurrence. The architecture is the basis of BERT, the GPT models and most large language models since, and Katharopoulos et al. (2020) later described a linear-attention variant under the name 'linear Transformer'.

claim.summary: Schmidhuber says his 26 March 1991 report on 'fast weight controllers' described a slow network that learns by gradient descent to generate key-like and value-like patterns whose outer products program the weights of a fast network. He says this is mathematically what is now called an unnormalized linear Transformer, apart from the normalization. He adds that a 1993 follow-up used the word 'attention', that the 2017 quadratic Transformer combines the 1991 additive outer-product principle with a softmax, and that the 2017 paper did not cite the 1991 work. The 2021 ICML paper by Schlag, Irie and Schmidhuber states the formal equivalence.

response.summary: Vaswani and colleagues describe the Transformer as the first transduction model based entirely on attention, without recurrence or convolution. Their paper combines multi-head softmax attention, positional information and feedforward layers, and cites LSTM and earlier memory architectures but not the fast weight papers. The later equivalence result by Schlag, Irie and Schmidhuber concerns linearized attention, rather than the entire softmax-based 2017 architecture. The linked sources contain no direct reply by the 2017 authors to the 1991 claim, so that result establishes a mathematical relationship without itself establishing historical influence or identity between the complete models.

agreed_facts: Schmidhuber's technical report FKI-147-91, 'Learning to control fast-weight memories: An Alternative to Dynamic Recurrent Networks', is dated 26 March 1991, and the journal version appeared in Neural Computation 4(1) in 1992.
Vaswani et al. posted 'Attention Is All You Need' on arXiv on 12 June 2017 and presented it at NIPS 2017.
The 2017 paper cites Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's 1997 LSTM paper and a 2001 gradient-flow paper co-authored by Schmidhuber, and it does not cite the 1991 or 1992 fast weight papers.

Katharopoulos et al. introduced the term 'linear Transformer' at ICML 2020 and do not cite the fast weight papers, and Schlag, Irie and Schmidhuber published 'Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers' at ICML 2021.
Softmax attention in the 2017 Transformer has costs that grow quadratically with sequence length, while linearized attention scales linearly, and Schmidhuber's own page makes the same distinction.
crux: Whether a system with softmax attention, as in the 2017 Transformer, counts as a variant of a 1991 system with additive outer-product memory and no softmax, which Schmidhuber's group has shown equivalent to linear attention only 'apart from normalization'. A second question is whether leaving the 1991 report out of the 2017 reference list, and out of later linear-attention papers, was a failure to credit earlier work or a reasonable reading of what was new.
